blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Decode the task’s role, form, audience and purpose; write 150–200 words whose vocabulary, style and structure fit them.

blocks.heading: Writing in a given style
blocks.text: Writing in the style of a text means taking on its register, its sentence patterns, its voice and its signature features, so a continuation reads as if the same writer wrote it. The style is found by naming it: its register (formal, conversational), its typical sentence (long and subordinated; short and clipped), its voice (ironic, confiding), and two signature features (the aside in dashes; the rule-of-three close). Held in mind together, they are the style; guessed at, they are a costume.

blocks.heading: Decoding the task
blocks.text: A directed-response task is decoded before the first sentence is written, and the decode runs in order. The role: who am I — a resident, the head learner, a visitor? The form: what kind of text — a speech, a letter, a blog? The audience: who reads it — the hall, the editor, friends? The purpose: what must it do — persuade, inform, celebrate? And what must come from the source: which facts, which viewpoint. Writing as the role is different from writing about it: the role’s voice speaks, sees from its own position, and never steps outside to report itself.

blocks.heading: Sharing out the words
blocks.text: The 150–200-word range is part of the task, and the words are shared out: an opening that establishes the form’s convention and the role’s voice; a body that carries the source’s content in two or three developed moves; a close that lands the purpose. The form’s conventions are the skeleton — a speech addresses its audience and closes memorably, a letter salutes and signs off — and a response missing them is a poorer fit to the task whatever its content.

blocks.heading: Worked example: the role decides the voice
blocks.text: A task sets a letter to a railway manager proposing a school visit, from a teacher, re-using a brochure’s content. The role — a teacher — decides the voice: practical, fond of the class, and accountable ("our Year 10 group of thirty-one, including two learners with mobility needs"). The audience — a manager — decides the register: polite, specific, easy to answer. The purpose — to secure a visit — decides the close: dates offered, a request for a reply. Every sentence could only have been written by that teacher to that manager, which is the test of a directed response.

blocks.heading: Where the task sits
blocks.text: The directed response is Section A of Paper 1, and its part (b) — the comparison taught in the next two sections — is written about the text this task produces, which is why the response’s choices matter twice: once for the ten marks of this task, and once as one half of the fifteen that follow. A response with clear conventions and a chosen register gives the comparison something to analyse; a lifted summary gives it almost nothing. Write the response as a text, not a paraphrase, and the comparison thanks you.

blocks.heading: Length and conventions
blocks.text: Two errors cost the writing marks. Writing far more, or far less, than 150–200 words is a poorer fit to the form and purpose — the range is judged as part of the task, not as a rule with a penalty attached, and an answer well outside it has less room to develop or has sprawled past its reader. And leaving out the form’s conventions — the speech with no address to its audience, the letter with no salutation — asks the reader to guess the form, which the task asked the writer to show.
